extracted.intended_audience: judge advocates, military contracting officers, and government lawyers
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and legal standards governing military communications (orders, notices, channels, official envelopes) and federal government contracts (parties, advertising, bidding, exceptions, performance, assignments, remedies). Aimed at advising legal/administrative action in military and federal procurement contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption as to War Department orders
rubrics_metrics.description: General or special orders relating to the Army, issued from the War Department by the Secretary of War or by his direction, are to be presumed to be made by the authority of the President and to be viewed as his orders equally as if he had subscribed the same.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat War Department orders as presidential orders for legal effect. (R. 8, 297, Apr., 1864.)

rubrics_metrics.name: When an order becomes operative / constructive notice
rubrics_metrics.description: An order becomes operative, and a military person is chargeable with notice of it, when it is shown that the order has been forwarded in the regular way to an officer's regiment, where it will be presumed to have reached its destination and been delivered to the officer unless he was absent from his regiment; constructive delivery can occur if the officer was absent without authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General orders: operative as to a command on the date of receipt by the command; if date of receipt cannot be ascertained, use date of the order. Special/individual orders: operative when served upon or received by the person through usual military channels. A soldier cannot be held criminally responsible under a general order after its date but before knowledge could have reached his command.

rubrics_metrics.name: Future-dated orders and detailed assignments
rubrics_metrics.description: Orders issued detailing officers for duty that become operative at a future date do not operate to detach the officer from his organization or post of duty until it becomes time for him to start for his new post in order to comply with the order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An assignment of a successor relieves the incumbent on the date the successor enters upon the duty under the order even if the local commander omitted to issue a relieving order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retroactive (nunc pro tunc) orders and ratification limits
rubrics_metrics.description: An order cannot create a fact to-day and carry it back to some prior date as if it occurred then; however, a legally retroactive executive order or ratification can validate prior acts when approval by the Secretary of War (or higher authority) is required and subsequently given.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between illegal attempt to manufacture past facts and lawful ratification: superior may ratify ministerial/executive acts he could have delegated at the time they were done, but not acts beyond his authority (e.g., judicial or discretionary powers that cannot be delegated).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and limits of penalty envelopes
rubrics_metrics.description: The legend 'Penalty for private use — $300' on an official envelope constitutes a sufficient statement required by statute; penalty envelopes may be used in the discharge of official duty by officers of the United States Government and under certain limited circumstances by recruiting officers and state adjutants general assisting with muster-in of volunteers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Penalty envelopes may not be used for private matters. They cannot be enclosed by an officer in a letter to a contractor for returning signed vouchers. Users must decide legality case-by-case, mindful of criminal liability for misuse. Authorities of external institutions (e.g., colleges) cannot initiate use, but may forward documents in penalty envelopes previously furnished by the department.

rubrics_metrics.name: Telegrams and public business exception
rubrics_metrics.description: A telegram recommending extension of furlough sent by a post commander did not fall within the prohibition of Army Regulations where it related to public business and did not originate with the beneficiary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Communications by telegram may be treated as public business where the subject and the origin are official; verify regulation prohibitions before sending.

rubrics_metrics.name: Channels of communication: military vs nonmilitary
rubrics_metrics.description: Military channels are to be used for official business; use of nonmilitary channels to influence the War Department is a violation of Army Regulations and may warrant notation on efficiency records. An officer outside Washington may furnish information directly to a Congressional committee, but an officer stationed in Washington must forward replies through military channels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not attempt to influence departmental action via nonmilitary channels. Geography and duty station can affect permissible direct communications with Congress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parties to contracts and proper signing
rubrics_metrics.description: Guidance on who may be a party to a government contract (United States, contractor, executors, assignees, government agencies) and on signing: where the name recited in the body varies from the actual signatory, rules apply; executors and assignees should sign in their own names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an individual conducts business under a company name, contract and bond should be in the individual's name; government agencies/instrumentalities may contract with the Government; follow formal signing rules to avoid disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contracts by statute-specific officers cannot be delegated
rubrics_metrics.description: Where Congress imposes upon certain named officials the duty of making a contract, such duty cannot be delegated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If statute names the contracting official, ensure the named official performs/signs the contract or statutory invalidity issues may arise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contract with public officer in his official capacity does not bind him personally
rubrics_metrics.description: A contract made with a public officer in his official capacity does not create personal liability on the officer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure capacity is clear in the contract; if personal liability is intended, the contract must explicitly bind the individual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertising requirement under Section 3709 R.S. (scope and purpose)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 3709 (Revised Statutes) requires advertising (public notice) for certain government contracts; the scope, purpose, and sufficient description for advertisement are delineated and may be waived in limited circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the procurement falls within the statute; ensure advertisements contain sufficient description and comply with statutory requirements unless a permitted exception applies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptions to advertising requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Statutory and practical exceptions include: exigency (emergency), subject not supplies, subject is personal services, aggregate small amount (e.g., under $500 per act of June 12, 1906), competition would be useless (patented/copyrighted articles, rare maps), purchases from other departments or governmental agencies, supplemental/extra work under an existing contract, and where statute specifically permits alternatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carefully document the basis for an exception (who determined exigency, statutory citation). Supplemental contracts must be confined to the subject of the original and not against U.S. interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bids and bidders — lowest and lowest responsible bidder
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules about who is the lowest bidder and who is the lowest responsible bidder (including special rules for printing under specific acts), treatment of bids received after the opening hour, and whether a bidder is bound by terms of his bid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate both price and responsibility/qualifications of bidders; late bids are generally not accepted; letters accompanying bids may be considered part of the bid; failure to sign may be fatal unless substantial compliance; verbal authority to sign may be adequate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection, acceptance, and amendment of bids
rubrics_metrics.description: Readvertisement is equivalent to rejection of all bids not before accepted; acceptance of one bid constitutes rejection of all others; bidders may not make material amendments after bids have been opened; where all bids rejected, guarantors released; acceptance after expiration of time limit may not bind guarantors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat acceptance as final and control communications and any amendments before opening; exercise care when readvertising to understand legal effect on prior bids and guaranties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contractor not released when release would harm U.S. interest
rubrics_metrics.description: A contractor will not be released from a contract when such release would be against the interest of the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even where circumstances suggest relief, weigh U.S. interest; courts may not permit rescission if harmful to the Government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mistake and other grounds for nonperformance
rubrics_metrics.description: Mistake may be ground for releasing bidder or nonperformance in certain cases (e.g., mistake as to sample); other grounds include variances between contract and officer requirements, difficulty of performance is not an excuse, act of God may excuse, injunction/bankruptcy generally not excuses under specified rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze nature of mistake and contractual terms; statutory and case law determine whether excuse applies; do not assume contractor relief absent clear legal grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liability of bidders and guarantors (certified checks etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Guarantors' liability is strictly construed; certified checks may amount to substantial compliance; if bidder dies within time limit estate may not be bound; notice requirements in guaranties must be actual; acceptance after time limit may not bind guarantors; 'blanket' guaranties are sometimes legal; regulations requiring guaranties may be waived.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the guaranty terms strictly; treat certified checks and other payments per the law and contract instructions; consider legal consequences of withdrawal at different stages (before/after opening, before/after acceptance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Advances of public money (Section 3648 R.S.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Public money may be advanced under certain statutory directions (e.g., rent may be paid in advance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure statutory authorization for any advance and document purpose/authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contracts and expenditures in excess of appropriations (Section 3679 R.S. etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fiscal-year contracts and other contracts conditioned on future appropriations or imposing indefinite liability on the United States are unauthorized; various statutory provisions (sections 3679, 3732, 3733) and amendments govern permissible obligations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not execute contracts that legally bind the Government beyond appropriations or create unauthorized fiscal liabilities; check relevant statutes for exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment of contracts (Sections 3477 and 3737 R.S.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assignment statutes generally make certain assignments voidable but not void; statutory provisions define scope, instances void under section 3477, effect of assignment in bankruptcy/for creditors, and relationship to assignment of claims under a contract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish assignment of contract from assignment of claim; money due under contract generally payable to the original contractor only unless statutory exception applies; review contract provisions and statute before allowing or recognizing assignments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purchases forbidden from certain persons
rubrics_metrics.description: Purchases are forbidden from persons in the military service or where members of Congress are interested under Army Regulations and sections of the Revised Statutes, though some provisions are directory only or have specified exceptions (e.g., approvals by Secretary of War, purchases from corporations in which officers hold stock, transactions with wives carrying on independent business).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply statutory prohibitions and regulatory exceptions carefully; determine whether prohibition is directory or mandatory in each context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contracts to be in writing and signed at the end (Section 3744 R.S.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Contracts must generally be in writing and signed at the end as required by section 3744; in the absence of a written contract recovery for failure to perform is limited, and certain exceptions (e.g., act of June 12, 1906) apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure written contracts when statute requires; where performance begins under an accepted bid and contract is later refused approval, bidder may be payable for work performed under limited circumstances; follow formal signing requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Returns, oaths, set-offs, and withholding moneys due contractor
rubrics_metrics.description: Statutory rules govern office returns, oaths (section 3745), set-offs, and the Government's right to withhold moneys due a contractor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use statutory procedures when asserting set-off rights or withholding payments; ensure required oaths and returns are taken where statute requires.

rubrics_metrics.name: Damages, liquidated damages, and penalties
rubrics_metrics.description: Provisions for forfeiture or penalty, reduction in price as penalty, forfeiture of retained percentages, provisions treating damages for failure as penalty, and the treatment of forfeiture of certified checks as penalties are detailed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft and interpret damages clauses carefully; courts will scrutinize whether contractual provisions are penalties or enforceable liquidated damages; consider whether provisions secure actual damages or are punitive.
